![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230684/assets/c4e47604540f3cfb3f73af34b0d3eb64bb649e9a42004d22eccc2dd9007de4fb.png)

Consider the vector field $F=2x\,i+y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230684/assets/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=16.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(2x\,i+y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+2\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 16+2\cdot 8=48.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=3xy\,i-{x}^{2}\,j$ and the circle $C$ given by ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ If the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\boxed{}\,\text{d}s,
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ is $n=x\,i+y\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230684/assets/386f010932b5846e7f47a605a94a5b5d580bd35dbe37512b1583d15d29f3dc70.png)

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(3xy\,i-{x}^{2}\,j)\cdot (xi+y\,j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}2{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is $2{x}^{2}y.$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i-{x}^{2}y\,j$ and the square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ shown above. If the flux of $F$ across the side ${C}_{4}$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\boxed{}\,\text{d}s,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

In our case, we need to find an expression for the flux across only the part ${C}_{4}$ of the closed curve $C.$ Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $n=-j.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230684/assets/c591fedf1b1c8ea705f0c13fbfd96bc7f1f6701841e3eff03bd0578aa2f8ab06.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i-{x}^{2}y\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${x}^{2}y.$

Consider the vector field $F=-3\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230684/assets/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

Now, since the vector field $F=-3\,j$ is parallel to ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through ${C}_{2}$ will cancel with the net outflow through ${C}_{4}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s\,⟹\,{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230684/assets/5c8aef7238da3bb5aed0fd2a458f6fd9bcd42884bbd350616e58e7a25b1f0fe2.png)

Consider the vector field $F=-2x\,i-2y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230684/assets/878a9992405e5968a03a04d12f42aeb85bca52c07dc7081244b04011643a74bf.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-2x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=3\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-3}^{3}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =-6(3-(-3)) \\  & =(-6)\cdot 6 \\  & =-36.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot (-36)=-144.
$$
